intro: A retrieval system returns three near-duplicate passages. Each may match the query, but the answer context wastes its limited space. Select a useful mix using relevance and redundancy together.
task: Return a list of k document indices using the stated maximal marginal relevance rule. Seed with the highest relevance; then repeatedly maximize weight*relevance[i] - (1-weight)*max(similarity[i,j] for j already selected).
requirements: relevance is a nonempty vector and similarity is a matching square matrix. Both contain finite scores in [0,1]. similarity must be symmetric with diagonal one (tolerance 1e-8).
k is a Python int with 0 <= k <= number of documents; bool is invalid. weight is a finite scalar in [0,1].
Resolve exact score ties by smaller original index. Never select an index twice. The first choice uses relevance even when weight is zero; k=0 returns [].
Recompute each remaining candidate's maximum similarity to the entire selected set after every choice. Preserve inputs; reject invalid arguments with ValueError.

examples.name: Relevance alone
examples.input: same scores and similarities, k=2, weight=1

hints.title: Separate the first choice
hints.body: There is no selected set at the start. Use the contract's relevance-first seed, then apply the redundancy penalty.

hints.title: Use the closest selected document
hints.body: A candidate redundant with any chosen passage deserves a penalty. Use the maximum similarity, not the average.

hints.title: Keep ordering deterministic
hints.body: Iterate candidates in ascending index order and retain the first candidate on an exact tie.

explanation: MMR makes selection depend on what is already in the result set. Once one passage is selected, a near duplicate receives a larger redundancy penalty.

This lesson supplies scores so you can inspect the selection rule without depending on an embedding model. Higher weight emphasizes query relevance; lower weight emphasizes diversity after the relevance-first seed.

This is a greedy procedure, not a guarantee of the globally best subset. Its outcome depends on score scaling and the candidate pool. Similarity alone also does not establish factual support for an answer.

For the first example, calculate both remaining candidates' scores by hand after choosing document zero. Then set weight to one and explain why the near duplicate returns. Compare the resulting context with rank fusion, which combines rankings but does not explicitly penalize redundancy.
formula: score(i | S) = λ · relevanceᵢ − (1 − λ) · maxⱼ∈S similarityᵢⱼ
